5.115.m: Śrī Rāma said: "When there was a confluence of a multitude of sins in the lowest of brāhmaṇas, / how did the Purāṇa-knower deliver the exposition, O best of the twice-born?"
Śambhu said: "Contact occurs in teaching and in studying; / in such contact, O Rāma, the sinner's sin transfers [to the other] for a year.
However, in the case of a Purāṇa-knower who understands the truth of all principles, O descendant of Kakutstha, / even a mass of sins accumulated as committed sin is destroyed.
Just as a cloud of smoke is extinguished by an abundant fire, / indeed, a moth is able to destroy a lamp, but not to destroy fire.
In that manner, the Purāṇa-reciter is capable of destroying sin committed by others. / Just as one possessing mantras who frees mortals seized by spirits and the like from the fear of spirits,
might cast it away so that he himself does not become afflicted, / even so the Purāṇa-reciter deserves to incur no sin whatsoever.
Whether sin has been committed by himself or by others, / the Purāṇa-knower destroys it, or his own exceedingly evil deed.
He has an equal attitude toward the Lord of Bhavānī and toward Hṛṣīkeśa; he is discerning, / knows the rites of the world and of the Veda, recites the Rudra-hymn, and is devoid of desire.
He is content, peaceful, skilled in ritual action, eminent, practicing yoga, and self-controlled. / Just as your Purāṇa-knower, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha,
remained in Ayodhyā by your command, O king; / he protected the entire earth, and when a rākṣasa rushed toward you,
that rākṣasa, guided by the instruction of Śukra, approached you thinking: / 'I shall kill him while he is attached to sleep; there is no other opportunity.'
Then the vipra Vasiṣṭha, who loved your welfare, knowing this, [thought:] / 'Undoubtedly, the rākṣasa will slay the descendant of Kakutstha when he is asleep and heedless.
He has obtained a boon from Brahmā, and his repulse must be carried out by me.' / Having considered thus, the sage among vipras set out taking an army.
Unable to kill the rākṣasa, who was free from death, the great sage / himself then assumed the form of a rākṣasa and spoke these words:
'For what purpose have you come here to this forest frequented by sages?' / He said, 'I have come to slay that king who destroys rākṣasas.'
The sage said to him, 'What is the use of his living or dying? / Eat my meat instead, fight, and attain victory!'
The rākṣasa said, 'How can you, being a rākṣasa, become food for me?' / Thereupon Vasiṣṭha, assuming human form, stood in the sky.
Spitting on his head, he struck him with his fist. / Struck by him, the rākṣasa fled, and the sage pursued him.
Both of them, running after each other, went to the ocean; / then that rākṣasa was seized by an aquatic creature living there.
The sage once again took up his residence in Ayodhyā as before. / Śambhu said: Therefore, an unselfish Purāṇa-knower should act according to his wish.
And I will describe the auspicious regulation for listening [to it]; listen! / In the bright fortnight, on a pure day, according to the conjunction of weekday and lunar mansion,

in a proper astrological division (karaṇa) and ascendant (lagna) endowed with the strength of planets and lunar mansions, / when no planet is combust, neither young nor old, and when Jupiter is properly situated,
not in the dark fortnight, nor during an eclipse, nor in the presence of an atheist, / one should listen to the Purāṇa endowed with the characteristics mentioned before."
In a pure house, or on a pure altar-ground, or in a monastery, / on a riverbank, in a temple, or in an assembly hall,
or in a pleasant street-monastery or charitable hall, O Rāghava, / one should personally pay homage to the eminent twice-born, especially to the knower of the Purāṇa.
One should prepare an elevated seat for him, distinguished above all; / one should say gently, ‘Come to the seat of dharma.’
On the day of beginning the Purāṇa, one should declare what is to be done; / one should worship the expounder of the Purāṇa with garments and the like.
Having given auspicious, fine, and new garments, / ornaments for the hands and neck, vessels, and a seat,
and worshipping him with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains, and offering betel, / one should meditate on Viṣṇu wearing white garments, moon-coloured, four-armed,
with a serene face, for the pacification of all obstacles; / and having honoured the members of the assembly, one should then pray to Gaṇeśa.
Worship is performed with the mantra beginning with ‘Namaḥ’ and praise of Bhāratī; / in the morning one should commence the recitation of the Purāṇa.
On the opening day, O Rāma, three, five, or ten auspicious verses [should be recited]; / on the second day, twice that number are auspicious;
on the third day, O Rāma, more than that is desired; / through an unbroken succession of days, exposition and listening are thus [continued].
When the settled arrangement is established, then, having offered betel and the like / to the guru who recites the Purāṇa, one should listen again on the following day.
The Purāṇa should be heard thus day after day: such is the sacred tradition. / Whatever person hears the Purāṇa in the form of a vow,
wherever that Purāṇa is, there he goes, without a doubt. / Even if only a single verse is heard by one desiring to hear the Purāṇa,
it destroys the sin committed on that very day, without a doubt.
And he who listens to the Purāṇa in this way is freed from the bond of sin caused by killing a brāhmaṇa, / drinking liquor, stealing gold, or violating the wife of a guru, O Rāma.
And other sins committed by men in the past all perish; / even those acquired over a hundred years in this life perish for the listener as well as the speaker.
In the Kali age, all-knowingness does not exist among all brāhmaṇas; / therefore, even a flawed exposition bears fruit, just like an act of giving.
Vyāsa knows the intention of the Purāṇas, and no other; / and I know it especially, even better than Vyāsa and Brahmā.”

Neither Vedic recitation nor asceticism, neither mantra nor oblations
bring such fruit in the Kali age as listening to a Purāṇa.

By hearing even one, great sin indeed
meets destruction without doubt, as if by dwelling on Śrīśaila.

Therefore, the teacher who knows the Purāṇas is to be revered by the hearer, destroying sins;
there is no higher teacher than him who grants liberation.

Those who are gurus in mantras, and those considered gurus in the Vedic scriptures,
are not capable of giving all knowledge; therefore they are not [true] instructors.

Those who know the Vedic mantras often [become] goblins,
O Rāma, named brahmarākṣasas; therefore one should look upon the knower of the Purāṇa [as superior].

One averse to the Purāṇas certainly does not see everything;
therefore, the knower of the Purāṇa is a benefactor, the master who destroys sins.

Worship of him is worship of all; harming him is harming all;
just as among all gifts the gift of knowledge is praised,

so too the narrator of the Purāṇa is blessed; a gift to him yields great fruit.
Rāma said: What should be given to a narrator of the Purāṇa, how much, and of what kind?

What kind of Purāṇa is to be avoided, and what kind of Purāṇa-knower is to be avoided?
Śambhu said: Food and drink of six tastes, and oily substances,

and a house with its furnishings, O Rāma, one should cause to be given to the Purāṇa-knower;
all [these] in sufficient quantity, or even more, because of greater fruit.

Furthermore, one should give wealth, accompanied by clothes, beautiful and soft;
one should offer ornaments according to worth, to the best of one's ability.

Fragrance and flowers daily, or simply fragrance alone,
and simply flowers alone, and at the time of fruits, even fruits.

One should likewise offer betel, and bow down with devotion;
and at the completion of a Purāṇa, one should likewise give gifts and so forth.

Moreover, land, gold, and the like should be given in greater quantity, O king;
nor should anyone undertake to listen in silence [without offering anything].

Whatever worship is done by the members of the assembly, or done by a single individual,
worship is desired according to one's ability, by everyone, as in a place of god.

At a sacred ford also, O Rāma, and in sacred temples,
one should perform worship to the best of one's ability for the knower of the Purāṇa, O Rāghava.

The characteristics of a listener were stated by me earlier, O king;
now I shall tell you all the characteristics of a Purāṇa-narrator:

one devoid of noble birth, afflicted with severe disease, a great sinner, one condemned,
one devoid of clean conduct, one who has abandoned the Vedas and Smṛtis,

devoted to another god, foul-mouthed, deformed in limb or with extra limbs,
husband of a woman previously married to another, a thief, a killer of living beings, formless—[all these are to be avoided].

Now I will tell you which Purāṇa is to be avoided, O best of kings;
that which is spoken by ancient knowers, and that which has been proclaimed by other sages,

that which Vyāsa and other best of sages have spoken, that one should recite;
one should read the text contained in the Purāṇa and explain it, reflecting [on its meaning],

in any language whatsoever, O Rāma, from local vernaculars;
[yet] one does not attain the fruit by hearing a book composed in a vernacular.

Some exposition, O descendant of Kakutstha, is beneficial for the Purāṇa, indeed;
therefore, ask, O lord, for whatever Purāṇa I shall expound."

Śambhu said: Having thus heard what was spoken by the narrator of the Purāṇa, Gautama himself
gave three garments to that great-souled brāhmaṇa.

He first heard the Kūrma Purāṇa, so it has been heard by us;
he gave much gold and auspicious garments.

Then he heard the Liṅga, the Viṣṇu, and the Vāmana,
the Padma, the Garuḍa, the Saura, and the Brahma.

Thus Gautama heard those eight Purāṇas;
then he [heard] the Rāmāyaṇa, and the Kūrma once again.

Always indeed he repeated the mantra, "Śiva-Nārāyaṇa";
he attained death, and he went to the realm of Brahmā.

Brahmā, having honored that brāhmaṇa, then went to the world of Viṣṇu;
honored by Viṣṇu, he then went to the abode of Śiva.

That Gautama, the best of sages, is worthy of praise by all.
And the rules that were declared by me regarding listening to the Mahābhārata,

which was composed of old by the sage Vyāsa in three years, auspicious—
from hearing it completely, he who is an expounder of the Mahābhārata

should not bow down to any brāhmaṇa except the highest yogin;
he who expounds the Mahābhārata is worthy of worship by everyone.

He who daily expounds or reads the Mahābhārata—
that brāhmaṇa is superior to all, and he delivers human beings.

And he who expounds a single book, or all of them, or a few,
is freed from all sins and excels in [receiving] offerings to gods and ancestors.

To that brāhmaṇa alone should one bow down; him alone should one worship as worthy;
him alone should one feed daily; everything should one offer to him.

The rule for worshipping him is declared: at the time of exposition, the twice-born
is to be revered, or one should worship him with garments and the like according to the prescribed manner.

At the conclusion of the Ādiparvan, one should give three fine garments,
and gold according to one's means; at the Sabhāparvan, two garments.

At the Anuśāsanaparvan, Āraṇyakaparvan, and Svargārohaṇaparvan,
the worship is the same as the worship at the Ādiparvan, O bull among kings.

At the Karṇa, Aśvamedha, Virāṭa, Śalya, and Droṇa parvans,
three pure fine garments, or else two gold coins [should be given].

At the other minor parvans, one should bring two gold coins;
and at the Harivaṃśa, three garments accompanied by a gold coin.

At the conclusion of the entire Mahābhārata, one should be a giver of land;
at the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa, one should worship at book after book.

One should cause sufficient land or even gold to be given
to the expounder of the guru's word; he is the destroyer of all impurities.

Wealth, righteousness, pleasure, and liberation, O best of kings—
all these succeed from hearing the exposition, and [men] become wise.

It is the destruction of all sins, beginning with the killing of a brāhmaṇa;
by a single hearing of it, what has not been heard by men on earth?

With conveyances, wealth, gold, and the like, one should daily worship this
expounder, since from him comes the destruction of the mass of sins.

The other Purāṇas too, spoken by sages, they also
serve for the destruction of the sins of listeners, and especially of the narrator.

And he who proclaims all thirty-six Purāṇas
or listens to them, his heart never suffers sorrow.

The Brahma Purāṇa is stated as the first; the second is called the Padma;
the third is the Viṣṇu, and the fourth is called the Śiva;

then the Bhāgavata is declared as the fifth; the Bhaviṣya is stated as the sixth;
and the Nāradīya is proclaimed as the seventh;

the Mārkaṇḍeya is declared as the eighth; likewise the ninth,
the Āgneya; the Brahmavaivarta is proclaimed as the tenth;

the Liṅga, the Vāmana, the Skanda, and the Matsya;
the Kūrma, the Vārāha, or the Garuḍa is declared;

and the Brahmāṇḍa: the wise know these as the eighteen Purāṇas.
And likewise, I shall tell the secondary Purāṇas hereafter:

The first is called Sanatkumāra; after that, the Narasiṃha;
the third is designated as Māṇḍa, and then the Daurvāsasa;

then another Nāradīya, the Kāpila, the Mānava,
likewise the Auśanasa is declared, and after that the Brahmāṇḍa;

the Vāruṇa, the one called Kālikā, the Māheśa, and the Sāmba,
the Saura, the Pārāśara, the Mārīca, and that called Bhārgava.
and the Kaumāra. Thus eighteen Purāṇas have been proclaimed; / and Manu became the expounder of the eighteen Purāṇas.

5.116.m:
Sūta said:
"Let the performance of the evening twilight worship be done," said Rāma to the sage.
"The hot-rayed [sun] is setting; this flock of birds is returning to its nest."

Desiring to perform his evening twilight worship, he himself went toward the northern direction, having left his conveyance,
with song performed by Hāhā and Hūhū, and his fame proclaimed by bards and chiefs.

Having reached the bank of the Gautamī, Rāghava, whose pair of feet was well washed by the son of the wind,
his hand held by Jāmbavat, reached the excellent river Gautamī.

With kuśa grass held in both hands, Rāghava then first went toward the excellent direction of Varuṇa.
Having offered the threefold libation according to the rules, his hair bristling with joy, he then muttered [prayers] inwardly.

The sky was as if smeared with nectar by the laughing rays of the moon,
with bright stars like flowers, like a canopy spread on all sides.

Then the king went to the roof of the palace prepared by his aged minister;
he went to the assembly hall furnished with various seats.

Then, having seated the sage, Rāghava himself took the chief seat;
the hosts of monkeys, huge in body, took their positions around him in order.

Observing the king seated comfortably, Śambhu, that good twice-born, spoke suitable words:
"Remaining here, you are worshipped by all; how is it, O best of kings, that the story remains in a cave?"

Then, having heard the words of the twice-born, the bearer of Raghu's line was eager to hear the story; / remaining there, he skillfully prevented speech, and it was heard by all in that instant.

"I wish to hear the story because of its great wondrousness, but it concerns myself differently,
telling of the torment of the rākṣasa." Then the king said, "What is this?"

"The killing of Kumbhakarṇa took place first, and the ten-headed [Rāvaṇa] met his death / afterwards—thus he recounts the Rāmāyaṇa composed in a different order."

Who is this best of brāhmaṇas who brings about unbelief among all people?
Coming to the place of kings, he speaks contrary to propriety. Is he to be punished or worshipped?"

Then Jāmbavat spoke to that best of the Raghus concerning the story: / "This Rāmāyaṇa is not yours; indeed, it is regarded as an invention."

O lord, I will tell you everything here in full; listen to that.
Formerly it was heard by me from the son of the lotus-born [Brahmā]."
Having addressed Jāmbavat, Rāmacandra spoke these words:

The glorious Rāma said:
"Proclaim the ancient tale to me; out of curiosity I am eager to hear. By whom was it composed and understood?"

Jāmbavat then said:
"Homage, homage to the Creator, and likewise to the moon-adorned [Śiva] and Keśava!
Now I will relate the ancient Rāmāyaṇa,

by hearing which there occurs the destruction of sins accumulated throughout all births.

Then nevertheless, Daśaratha, a charioteer equal to ten charioteers, wishing to conquer the city named Sumānasa with a vast army, summoned Vasiṣṭha, the son of the lotus-born [Brahmā]'s son, bowed to him, and with the sage's permission, accompanied by an army of a hundred akṣauhiṇīs,
mounted a horse whose body was like the moon, and seized with immense wrath, worshipped Viṣṇu and set out on a military expedition.
A king named Sādhya, surrounded by his own army, came facing Daśaratha to fight, and a battle took place between them.
Having fought for a month, Daśaratha captured that Sādhya.
Then Sādhya's son, named Bhūṣaṇa, having a small retinue, fought with Daśaratha.
Seeing Sādhya's son, an ornament of the earth, Daśaratha did not wish to fight at all.
"How can I kill such a boy? And if he is killed, how will his father survive? How will his mother survive? How will his noble beloved, whose youth is not yet fully grown, survive?
For on his body, marks of embracing, kissing, and rolling, like fresh lotus petals, are seen like flowers.

A son of equal complexion and age to this, so charming, who increased my utmost delight, was eaten and killed by a bear; though coming to my memory, he seems to wish to protect me, and turns my heart to sorrow." Reflecting thus in his mind, he set about to capture the boy.
And that Sādhya too had become subject to another.
He, together with the prince, disregarded the distress of defeat and dwelt in comfort.
Daśaratha also, having stayed there for a month, and observing the joy of beholding his son, thought:
"Ah, beholding this face is capable of removing all sorrow, as is raising a son! My victory over all kingdoms brings only sorrow to me who remembers the loss of my son.
Therefore I will ask him: how is such a son born?" Having deliberated thus, he asked him.

Sādhya then pointed out to the king the path of complete liberation:

"Having worshipped Hari and Īśāna together, having fasted on all the eleventh-day [observances], having honored brāhmaṇas on the twelfth-day [observances] with seasonal fruits,

food, condiments, and flowers obtained righteously, having bathed Keśava with ghee from a brown cow, having anointed him with mung bean powder,

having bathed him with fresh water, having smeared all the limbs of the deity with fragrant sandalwood paste rubbed by oneself, mixed with musk and the essence of agallochum,

and having worshipped according to one's means with tulasī leaves, jasmine, oleander, blue water-lilies, lotuses, red water-lilies, droṇa flowers, maruva, damanaka, girikarṇikā, and ketakī petals,
having worshipped with the twelve-syllable mantra or the Puruṣasūkta or with names and sixteen services, having bowed down and danced, one should beg forgiveness of the deity.
Likewise, one should perform various vows for the pleasing of Nārāyaṇa.
When pleased, the divine sage bestows the desired son; therefore worship him," he said to Daśaratha.
And he, having installed Sādhya there, went to Ayodhyā and did everything accordingly.

Then, when the sacrifice for obtaining a son was completed, the embodiment of the sacrifice, holding a conch, discus, and mace in his hands, arose from the āhavanīya fire and said to the king, "Choose a boon."
And the king chose: "Grant four sons who are exceedingly righteous, long-lived, and benefactors of the worlds."
Then the king's four chief queens, Kauśalyā, Sumitrā, Surūpā, and Suveṣā,
said to the king: "O lord, there should be one son to each wife."
Then Kauśalyā said: "If this divine being is pleased, let him be born to me."

The king said: "If it is my wish, then Hari is prayed to:
'O Viṣṇu, be gracious, O Lord of gods, O husband of Kamalā, O bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, whose pair of feet is worshipped by Vibhīṣaṇa, the creation, and all world-protectors, O eternal Hari, homage to you, homage to you!' Praised thus, the Lord then said to the king:
Mādhava said: “I will become your son through Kauśalyā.” / Then Hari entered the sacrificial oblation [caru]. / Having divided that caru into four portions, [the king] gave it to his wives.
Then Rāma was born to Kauśalyā, Lakṣmaṇa to Sumitrā, Bharata to Surūpā, / and Śatrughna to Suveṣā; and a shower of flowers fell from the sky.
Then the Four-faced One [Brahmā] himself approached and performed the rites such as the birth ceremonies.

Because he was pleasing to the three worlds, he gave him the name ‘Rāma’; because of his fitness for beauty, valor, and the goddess Lakṣmī, he named another ‘Lakṣmaṇa’; / because he delivers the earth from its burden, he gave the name ‘Bharata’; and because he slays enemies, ‘Śatrughna’. Having given these names, Brahmā went to his own abode, and the boys grew up.

Then, as [Rāma] walked on his feet, his appearance resembling the crescent moon, his lips like the bimba fruit, his nose like a raised sesamum blossom, with a crest-ornament hanging before him,

with jeweled leaf-ornaments dangling, with trembling earrings swaying at his ears, with a necklace of large pearls shifting on his chest, gleaming

with bracelets of gold, with jingling gem-studded wristlets and gem-set rings, with a waist-cord fashioned of gold and jewels, his feet adorned with jingling anklets,

with toe-rings adorning his toes and a ring on his middle toe, the broad soles of his feet adorned with the auspicious marks of the thunderbolt, the elephant goad, and the lotus,

his shanks resembling quivers, his thighs like elephants' trunks, his hips broad, his waist slender, his belly adorned with a round whirlpool-like

deep navel, his broad chest resembling a slab of sapphire, his neck like a conch shell, his face like the orb of the moon, his forehead like the half-moon, his dark curls locks of hair
his chest pale with dust adhering to his breast, his restless eyes reddish like the petals of a blossoming lotus, like Maheśvara covered in ashes,
skyclad [naked] like Maheśvara—seeing the young prince Rāma, King Daśaratha, / his heart brimming with joy, embraced his son, kissed him, and pressed him firmly to his chest.
Then the prince too, placed sideways upon his lap, his eyes darting pleasantly, uttered some indistinct words;

looking all around as he asked: “Father, let us go; let us sleep, father; I shall play, father!”—experiencing again and again such filial joy, [the king] attained deep satisfaction.

Then once, when the king had come to dine, Rāmacandra, his heart absorbed in childish play, with various toys in his hands,

came leaping and running, took with his left hand the food situated in the jewel-encrusted golden dish set before the king,
The king considered even this to be a joy. / Rāmacandra performed many other such playful acts.
Then once, while Rāma was playing, a whirlwind threw Rāma down, and weeping, Rāma fell.
At that moment, a brahmarākṣasa seized Rāma, and Rāma fell into a faint.
Then his companion, a boy crying loudly as he ran hither and thither, reported Rāma's condition to the king.
Then the king, taking Rāma, went to Vasiṣṭha and asked: “What has happened to Rāma?”
Then Vasiṣṭha took ashes, consecrated them with mantras, and released [Rāma from] the brahmarākṣasa.
He asked: “Who are you?” And he replied: “I was a brāhmaṇa proud of my Vedic knowledge. Having repeatedly stolen others' wealth, I became a brahmarākṣasa. Devise an expiation for me.”

Vasiṣṭha said: “Now, from here on, you must endure the hellish state of a rākṣasa for a hundred years; / having offered a hundred bilva leaves to Śiva, and then bathing in the Bhāgīrathī, you will be freed from sin.”

“I confer upon you the merit of some such good deed I have done; thereupon you will attain the highest goal.” Hearing Vasiṣṭha's word, by virtue of the merit bestowed by Vasiṣṭha, the brahmarākṣasa assumed a celestial body, bowed, and went to heaven.
Then, when the proper time arrived, Vasiṣṭha invested Rāma with the sacred thread and taught him the Vedas, the six auxiliary limbs, the two Mīmāṃsās, and the science of statecraft;
and then the science of archery, medicine, the arts of drama and music, architecture, the science of omens, and the various sciences of warfare.
Then King Daśaratha, wishing to arrange [Rāma's] marriage, dispatched messengers to the rulers of various regions.
Then a certain messenger arrived quickly and spoke thus to the king:

“O King, the ruler of the Vidarbha country is a king named Videha; his daughter, Vaidehī, obtained through a sacrificial offering, equal to Lakṣmī in beauty, endowed with all auspicious marks, is worthy of Rāma; and that king is eager to give her to Rāma. Therefore, go quickly!”

Then he sent Vasiṣṭha and others; and they, having gone there and seen her, determined the auspicious time for the marriage, returned to Ayodhyā,

and reported to the king. Accompanied by Rāma and together with the king, they set out quickly with various elephants, horses, carts, litters,

and palanquins. Skilled in graceful postures, charms, and amorous dalliance, knowing various arts, like Gandharva women, highly adept in the treatises on love, their soft, firm, and plump breasts resting close to their necks,

with lotus faces having broad and delicate foreheads and lips like bimba fruit, with braided masses of long hair with curly locks,

with ears adorned with golden leaves, with hair raised [in goosebumps] from the activity of bathing, their teeth [stained] red as hibiscus flowers, their eyes flashing like shining saphara fish,

with ears resembling oyster shells, their nostrils adorned with large pearls like stars, their cheeks smooth as mirrors, their noses like sesamum blossoms,

with nipples slightly sloping at the midpoint, their lips resembling indragopa insects and marked with tooth-bites,

their limbs evenly long and beautifully displayed, rounded in every part,

the roots of their arms resembling petals of the karṇikāra flower on account of fine hairs recently arisen and their golden complexion,

with soft, glossy, rounded, and slender waists, with firm, plump, rounded breasts having sunken nipples, seeming to vie with one another in occupying space,

with brooches resting between their breasts, their chests adorned with tremulous necklaces of diverse gems resting upon their breasts,

their abdominal regions adorned with a unique line of hair rising above the well of the navel, their waists capturable in a fist and beautified with three folds as if to prevent the midpoint from breaking,

their hip regions resembling elephants' trunks, their knees even, soft, glossy, and hairless,

his thighs resembling trunk-stems of plaintain trees, his knees sunken, slender with round and muscular calves,

with sunken ankles, with delicate, glossy, and very long toes, with the jingling sound of their anklets as if invoking the god of love,

the tuck of their lower garments touching their right big toes, fastening the upper tuck into a knot [nīvī], leaving their necks uncovered by the fold of cloth held by both hands,
their breast-cloth wrapped across the other portion of their garment, with the hem on the left shoulder itself passing along the right side
and tucked near the navel, their slender forms thus adorned—women arrived in great numbers to perform the auspicious rites of marriage.

adorned with thousands of garland-makers smiling gently with lips resembling japā flowers and wearing diverse pearl necklaces;

having residences for the preparation of sacred distilled liquors; with variegated archways here and there; clean streets; wish-fulfilling trees planted at various spots; and doorways decorated with plantain stems—in this manner he adorned the splendid city.

Then, to welcome [them], the king set forth with wanton women and other resplendent people, accompanied by women carrying golden vessels worthy of worship filled with diverse ornaments, ghee, bdellium, fruits, and other auspicious articles, their hair bound with turmeric, dūrvā grass, and unhusked barley, their eyes lined with collyrium, their braided hair adorned with knotted crests and parted hair-lines, and their faces and noses beautifully adorned.
At that time, the sounds of auspicious musical instruments arose: divine kettle-drums, bherī drums, niḥsāṇa drums, mardala drums, conches, and the like.
And singers sang auspicious songs.
Vedic Brahmins and reciters of family genealogies filled the entire sky with the recitation of auspicious Vedic passages and the booming of drums.
Then, mutually acknowledging one another as never before, praised by Sūtas, bards, and panegyrists, they entered the city.
Daśaratha entered the palace built in the western section of the city of Videha.
And the rest entered residences according to their rank.
Now Nārada arrived in Mithilā at that very moment.
The king of Videha, having worshipped the divine sage, having seen to his welcome and fed him, gave betel with camphor to the sage who sat comfortably, and addressed him:
“Tomorrow you ought to stay at the wedding to conduct the marriage.”
“Tomorrow the asterism is in conjunction with the sun; the wedding should not be performed under such an asterism.”
Then the king summoned the astrologer, the aged Gārgya, and asked: “Where is the auspicious moment for the wedding?”
Looking at both Nārada and Gārgya, the king asked: “O sirs, how is this?”
Then Nārada said to Gārgya:
“How will you determine an auspicious moment as you have stated?”
Then Gārgya said: “I will grant the moment by avoiding the inauspicious hours (viṣaghaṭikā).”
Nārada also said to Gārgya: “Do you not know the words of Brahmā?”
Then Gārgya recited those flaws:
“Meteors, the staff of Brahmā, futility, and earthquakes / were seen of old by Brahmā as causing the ruin of all undertakings.
In consecrations, in marriages, in investiture with the sacred thread, and in coronations, / and in all other enterprises, one should avoid the venomous hours (viṣanāḍī).
Beyond that, however, performing undertakings incurs no fault; / therefore, I speak only of the fault in marriages and similar rites.
A meteor burns down an entire lineage; the staff of Brahmā destroys it; / futility leads to death; an earthquake leads to the shaking of the undertaking.”
Hearing what Nārada said, the sage Gārgya became silent.
He meditated upon the Sun, the lord of the planets: “Let the wedding be performed, having avoided the venomous hours.”
Nārada said: “What of the word of Brahmā?”
The Sun said: “The rule has been stated according to regional differences. Therefore, in this region, the marriage is certainly to be performed by avoiding the inauspicious hours.”
He said: “Tomorrow afternoon there should be a kṣatriya marriage; therefore let the kings assemble for the svayaṃvara. Send messengers to those kings.”
Then the king, with the consent of Daśaratha, caused all the kings to assemble, and wondered: “How can the daughter of Videha be given to Rāma while disregarding all [the others]?”

fond of ghee and milk, fond of droṇa and oleander blossoms, fond of bilva leaves, fond of blue and red lotuses, fond of nandyāvarta, bakula, and jasmine flowers...

O giver of victory! O giver of the discus produced from the water when besought by Hari! O giver of the faculty of memory! O giver of auspiciousness to those who remember [you]! O conqueror of death! Homage to you!
Hearing this hymn of praise, the Blessed Bhava said to the king: “I grant boons; choose a boon.”

The king said: “O illustrious one, my daughter Vaidehī is intended to be given to Rāma in a svayaṃvara. If someone mightier than Rāma should take her in the gathering of all beings—numerous kings, Rākṣasas, Brahmins, and others endowed with noble lineage, beauty, strength, and vigor—then my word would prove false and a sin would be mine.

Moreover, Daśaratha also is capable of conquering all who arrive. If Rāma, who is a destroyer of the warrior class, should arrive, what will he do to my daughter, or what will he send, or what will he cause to be done, or what will he do to me? For in every way, a king endowed with abundant forces and mounts could destroy even all three worlds, not to speak of me of small strength. What need of many words? You alone are my refuge. Tell me a means whereby there will be auspiciousness in the marriage, and Rāma will become my son-in-law.”
Śambhu too said: “I shall do so.
Rāma alone will be Sītā's lord. / And having brought Rāma [here], I shall make prosperity this very day. Take this bow, the Ājagava.”
The king said: “What is to be done with this Ājagava bow? In the svayaṃvara, bring Sītā to Rāma.”
Śaṅkara said: / “This bow of mine is unstrung. Whoever strings it, / to him Sītā must be given by me. Make this vow.”
Having spoken thus, the Lord Hara disappeared with his hosts; / then the king, despite excessive exertion, was unable to lift the bow.

Then, summoning Ujjvala, who had the strength of a hundred thousand elephants, he said, “Take it.”

And he, having bowed to his maternal uncle, laughed aloud, leaped forward, and raised the bow with both hands up to his knees; his maternal uncle […]
Having heard, Mārīca alone, assuming the guise of a Brahmin, begged Videha: / “Know me to be a guest who has arrived at the end of the Vaiśvadeva rite.”
The king said: “Welcome, O Brahmin! Here is a seat, sit down there.”
And the guest said, “So be it,” and sat down.
Then the king, taking water, washed his feet, worshipped him with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, presented him with an offering, and invited him to a meal.

And he, looking at that food endowed with the six tastes and placed in a golden vessel, gazed here and there.

At that very moment, Sītā, wearing a slightly reddish garment with the radiance of lotus filaments, her forehead adorned with blue, curly locks of hair that moved, captivating the minds of young men, and as if displaying to watching eyes that the hearts of women were broken parts [of them],

with beautiful brows curved like the bow of the Bodiless One, with eyes red as lotus petals, with a nose like a sesame flower, with soft, glossy, and delicate cheeks,

with teeth like rubies and pomegranate seeds inside her reddish mouth and reddish lips, with a chin beautifully adorned by a lower lip red like a hibiscus flower,

with ears shaped like mother-of-pearl oysters, with an evenly proportioned long neck, with a very plump chest, adorned with numerous necklaces over her firm and swelling bud-like breasts,

of auspicious form, with very fleshy, creeper-like arms, with charming, long, and symmetrical tips of fingers, with hands like reddish lotus shoots,

with finger ornaments of various many-colored gems, with a waist that could be grasped by a fist, with a fine line of hair, with a deep navel, with broad hips, with thighs like elephant trunks, with shanks like quivers,
with lovely lotus-feet, with anklets and other foot-ornaments, with adorned toes, holding a blossoming saugandhika lotus—she came before the dining Mārīca.
Seeing her, he thought: “How can I abduct her? How can I embrace her? How can I do something else?” Finding no opportunity thus, he departed in silence.
Then the gods, striving to string the bow, pushing ahead of one another with mutual disdain, [tried]. Mahendra reached that supreme bow, but was not able to bend it beyond its two ends.
Then the Sun, taking up the bow, fell down while trying to bend it.
Then Vāyu, the best of the strong, seized the Ājagava; but as he drew it up with his own hand, he fell down, / and the bow fell on top of Vāyu; then all of them laughed.
Meanwhile, the thousand-armed Bāṇāsura, mounted on an excellent steed, surrounded by Daityas with many heads, arrived at the city of Videha together with Prahlāda.
Then, illuminating the directions with his own ornaments, making the gods dim by his own splendor, and listening to various songs, he had strength for only two finger-breadths and gave up.
Prahlāda and Bali then ran and ceased.
Then, when the Rākṣasas had fallen silent, very powerful kings arrived; unable to fasten the bowstring, they withdrew and stood aside. (126) / Then the Brahmins arrived.
Then Viśvāmitra took the bow, strung it up to one finger-breadth, and then ceased; / and the others turned back.
Then, when a whole day had passed and all were silent before the bow, Rāghava came with his younger brothers, inspected the bow, and touched it.
Then hundreds of princes arrived; / adorned with all ornaments, having seen the bow, they touched it, but were not capable of moving it.
Then the princes led by Daśaratha's son arrived.
Then guards holding canes and drums arrived and pushed everyone back.
Then Rāma, holding Lakṣmaṇa's hand, adorned with all ornaments, approached the bow, touched it, bowed, circumambulated it, took up the bow, and lifted it.
At that time of taking it up, all came and said laughingly, “Here the great chariot-warriors were broken!”
Then that Rāma bent the place for the bowstring, placed his knee upon the bow, brought forth the string with one hand, and bent it at the tip.
Then, seeing it strung, everyone placed their fingers to the tips of their noses [in astonishment].
Rāma, too, made the bowstring resound; / at that sound the minds of all were agitated.
Everywhere the report arose: "The bow has been strung by Rāma!"
Janaka, too, gave Sītā to Rāma; and fighting with the kings and conquering them, [Rāma] returned to his own city.

Then one day Daśaratha, having consecrated Rāma into the status of heir-apparent, became joyful; and because of the delight of all the subjects, the talk of all the subjects was: "Rāma is approved as king."
Then the daughter of the king of the Kaikeya country, well-adorned, not tolerating Rāma as king, said to the king: "It is time for the grant of my boon." The king thought: "What should be given?"
The queen said: "Let Rāma enter the forest for fourteen years; let Bharata rule the kingdom."
From fear of the fault of a false word, the king somehow accepted.
Then he said to Vasiṣṭha out of concern: "Rāma is departing for the forest. Deliberate and tell [me] what good or evil might become of him."
Having deliberated, Vasiṣṭha joyfully said to the king:

"Having gone to the forest, the slayer of all heroic Dānavas performs manifold worship of Śambhu; / and Rāma, enraged by separation from Sītā, crossing the ocean with an army of monkeys, slays the Ten-headed One.
Having returned to his kingdom, the delighter of the Raghu race rules for many years; / of celebrated renown throughout the entire world, he dwelt [there] long with the god Śarva.
Endowed with good sons, a performer of many sacrifices, he is a sovereign master, surpassing in all virtues."
Having heard those words of Vasiṣṭha, Daśaratha, recollecting the virtues of Rāma, spoke thus: "It would be better for me to die than for Rāma to depart."

Then Rāma, having bowed to his mother, father, and teacher Vasiṣṭha, and to his father's wives, departed for the forest.

Then, having stayed in a grove for one day, having made matted locks, having put on bark garments, having made [it] into a single sacred thread, having cleansed his teeth,

having tied his matted hair with a single sacred thread, all his limbs dusted with ash, his body hardened with ash, wearing on his chest a necklace of rudrākṣa beads interleaved with a strand of pearls,

Then he slew many rākṣasas there, as you know; he did everything—the abduction of Sītā and so forth—everything just as it occurred, O lord. Then Rāma went to the mountain Ṛṣyamūka, to Sugrīva's hermitage; approaching a mango tree with dense shade,

accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he constructed a shelter.

listening to the [forest] sounds, gazing at the fruit of the tree, [he saw] a monkey with jewelled earrings, golden-yellow, with a tightly bound loincloth of muñja grass, wearing a pure

sacred thread, extremely restless, taking fruit and throwing it at himself, scattering flower-clusters, imitating song, fanning Rāma with a fan, climbing a branch and likewise fanning him, bearing only a mango fruit. Seeing [him], Rāma addressed Lakṣmaṇa:
"Lakṣmaṇa, who is this monkey?"
Lakṣmaṇa said: "I do not know." / Then Rāma, calling [him] over, asked: "Whose [servant] are you? What is your name?"
And he said: "[I am] Sugrīva's [servant], Hanūmān."

Having bowed to Rāma, he approached Sugrīva, bowed, [and said]: "A young man, like another Lord Nārāyaṇa, dark as a cloud, with matted locks, whose arms reach his knees, exceedingly glorious, is staying here with another man who resembles the sun.
Then, seeing the two princes endowed with all auspicious marks standing under the shade of the tree, and told by them: 'Report to Sugrīva,' I have reported that to you."
Then Sugrīva quickly arose, took articles such as flowers and water, performed the washing of their feet and the like, offered fruits, and made an inquiry:
"Who are you two? Why have you come, princes [yet] ascetics?" Hearing Sugrīva's words, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, spoke:
"For that purpose we would cross the ocean, we would enter the underworld, we would master heaven, we would bring down mighty Indra, we would slay the powerful—we will do anything!"
‘This man's wife has been abducted by someone unknown; we two have come to search for her. That is indeed our main purpose; any other is secondary.’

Then Sugrīva, having made a mark, challenged Vālin to battle and stood ready.
