And Vālin fell, struck in the weapon-less fight by a blow of an arrow; then all his limbs were covered in blood.
Then Tārā and Aṅgada arrived and became distraught.
Then monkeys approached Rāghava, fell down near Vālin, and wept.
Then Tārā spoke to Rāma: "The descendants of Raghu were previously skilled in scripture, heroic, and righteous. How, O Rāma, did you commit a sin?
Do you not know the duty of the warrior class, practiced by hosts of kings?
When two fight with each other in battle, victory or death may occur; / if another should slay [one] of the two, he is declared a slayer of a brahmin.
Did you strike Vālin out of enmity, or out of a desire for monkey-meat?"
Did you kill Vālin out of enmity, or out of a desire for monkey-meat?

Monkey flesh is inedible. If out of personal grief and lack of happiness you think others must feel likewise—ah, or if this was done out of delusion to take me, what of your vow to have only one wife?

If Sugrīva was made an ally to bring back Sītā who was carried off by Rāvaṇa, what a great difference! When with Vālin, who is great in strength and full of goodwill, who can bring back Sītā in the time it takes the sun to rotate, who can bestow Rāvaṇa as a captive if remembered...

the king of monkeys, who possesses an army of fifty parārdhas of monkeys and bears, your purpose would have been accomplished. What can be accomplished by your purpose through Sugrīva, a monkey of little valor, a general of seven parārdhas, who merely makes promises?
Ah, it is known: may all be well with you, as you have spoken.

And Rāma says: 'As a ruler of the earth, I must punish the wicked and protect the righteous. By Vālin, Sugrīva's queen Rumā was abducted, and his kingdom too. Hence, there is no fault in killing such a one.'

Tārā said: 'Then Sugrīva too was fit to be killed! When Vālin, fighting with Dundubhi, entered the cave and dwelt there for a year, in the meantime Sugrīva abducted me and took the kingdom. Kill him first, and kill that other later!'
Rāma said: 'Tell me, how long ago was this?'
Tārā said: 'Within sixty thousand years, in the eightieth year, during the war with the rākṣasa, the kingdom was usurped by Sugrīva.
And after another year had passed, when Vālin arrived, Sugrīva fled.
His wife was taken, and the kingdom was taken away.
On that very day was the consecration of your father Daśaratha.'

Rāghava said: 'By the command of my father, I have punished the wicked within the kingdom, / for the word of an elder cannot be transgressed; whoever was king at the time of that abduction did not act.
Moreover, two animals are independent; Vālin was killed among animals. Nor is there blame for animals tearing each other to pieces.
For to me, hunting is [prescribed] by rule, or of beasts / moving, standing, trapped, running, wandering, or fleeing; / when one abandons attachment, hunting is likewise renounced.
This hunting was performed by me according to the rules of the treatises on hunting, / whether in sight or out of sight, running or not running.
From falling [into fault], the supreme state of the sattvic is preserved; / and for a king, hunting is duty even without the eating of meat.'
Then, having heard Rāma's words, they all shook their heads.
Placing his folded hands to his head, Vālin spoke to Rāma: 'Homage to you, Rāma! Listen to my words.
Holding the conch, discus, and mace, clad in yellow garments, teacher of the universe, / you yourself are Nārāyaṇa manifest—so I have heard.
Yogins meditate on you, and sacrificers offer sacrifices to you. / You alone consume the oblations to gods and ancestors, bearing the form of the ancestors and the gods.
For one who meditates on you at death, liberation is not far off. / Such as you are, you have come within my sight; O Rāma, my sins are destroyed!
Take back the arrow, O Kākutstha! I am in severe pain.'
Then Rāma, saying 'So be it,' withdrew the arrow and said to Vālin: 'Speak, what wish of yours should be granted?'
The monkey said: 'If the Lord is pleased, grant me a good realm after death.
Let this Sugrīva be protected, and likewise Aṅgada, and Tārā. A transgression was committed by sinful me, and I have experienced its fruit.'
Then, gazing upon Rāma, Vālin died and went to heaven.
Then, having consecrated Sugrīva in the kingdom, [Rāma] himself entered the forest.
Then, having gone near the ocean with him as his ally, Rāma said to Sugrīva: 'Where is Laṅkā? Where is Sītā? And where is the enemy?'
Then Hanumān said: 'Having entered Laṅkā, searched for Sītā, and learned the whole truth, battle or peace must be made. Therefore, let the Lord give some order for crossing the ocean.'
Then Rāma said to Sugrīva: 'How can this come to pass?'
The monkey said: 'I have monkeys by the crores, headed by bears.
Having appointed one, taking everything into consideration, what is fitting must be done.'
Then Jāmbavat said: 'Let Hanumān go alone; let him survey Laṅkā.'
Then Hanumān went, searched the city of Laṅkā, and having spoken with Sītā seated in the Aśoka grove and inspired confidence in her, destroyed the grove and the guardians of the grove.
Captured by the rākṣasa, he burned Laṅkā, went to the northern shore, saw Rāma, related the news, and stood silent.
Then Rāma deliberated with them all. Jāmbavat said: 'Nārada told me that Laṅkā will be destroyed by Rāma by means of monkeys.
Now effort must be made to cross the ocean.'

Then Rāma, having worshipped Śaṅkara, made all known to him, and spoken the words: 'I will do what you say,' worshipped Śiva, bowed down, and made his petition:

'O Mahādeva, devourer of the great elements, cause of the great dissolution, adorned with great serpents, Mahārudra, Śaṅkara, Supreme Lord!

O Virūpākṣa, wearing a serpent as sacred thread, clad in elephant hide, adorned with a heavy garland of skulls from Brahmā's heads,

adorned with human bones, covered in ashes, dear to the supreme Nārāyaṇa, of auspicious deeds, Pañcabrahman, primordial lord, five-faced one, four-faced one,

known through the Vedas, easily attained by devotees, difficult to attain by non-devotees, supreme bliss, highest consciousness, knock-out of Pūṣan's teeth, cutter of Dakṣa's head,

severer of Brahmā's fifth head, beloved of Pārvatī, whose auspicious deeds are sung by Nārada, Śarva, three-eyed one,

holding the trident, with the Pināka bow in hand, with matted locks, bearing many forms, mounted on a bull, resembling pure crystal, four-armed one,

bearing various weapons, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Lord, ruler of gods, bearer of the Gaṅgā, destroyer of Tripura, dweller on Śrīśaila, lord of Kāśī, ornament of Kedāreśvara,

lord of Siddheśvara, Gokarṇeśvara, Kanakhaleśvara, Parvateśvara, bestower of the discus, remover of anxiety for Bāṇa, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Murahara, Soma, adorned with the moon, omniscient, full of light, identical with the universe, homage to you, homage to you!'
As Rāma was thus praising him, an effulgent form arose before him from the midst of the liṅga.

Rāma then beheld the fearless Lord seated in the lotus posture, with Umā seated on his lap, wearing all ornaments, crowned with a lustrous diadem, touching Haimavatī's waist, bestowing fearlessness and boons with his two hands, radiant, filling all quarters with undulating light, with a smiling face and gracious countenance.
He bowed to the Supreme Lord with folded hands and fell prostrate like a staff.
Then the Supreme Lord also said to Rāma: 'Choose a boon; I am the giver of boons.'
Rāma said: 'I must go to Laṅkā. O Śambhu, give me a means to cross the ocean.'
Śambhu said: 'I have a bow named Ājagava, which takes the form of time and is unalterable. Mounting it, cross the ocean and reach Laṅkā.'
Rāma, deciding 'So be it,' remembered the Ājagava.
The bow arrived, and then Rāma worshipped it.
Then Hara took the bow and gave it to Rāma.
Rāma then cast it into the ocean.
All the monkeys and Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa mounted; sixty parārdhas of them, when countless monkeys mounted the bow, it did not bend as desired.
Then the monkeys, having gone there, examined the edge of the bow.
Then a rākṣasa named Atikāya, seeing the monkey army, spoke to Rāvaṇa.

Rāvaṇa also said: "What of the monkeys, tree-dwelling beasts? Or what of the two mortals, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa? Why have they come? Our food has arrived by fate!"

Then Sugrīva, while the sun was sinking in the west, along with mighty and gigantic [monkeys] in countless numbers led by Hanumān and Jāmbavat,

went to the side of Laṅkā, entered the garden, and having eaten various fruits,
they each took hold of the entire forest and rushed toward Laṅkā. Having reached the gateway, climbed up, and broken down the palace one by one, some took up pillars and fought with the rākṣasas.
Others demolished the halls, pulverized the houses, and slaughtered everyone—children, the elderly, women, and the rest.
Then Rāvaṇa, learning that one rampart had been subdued, dispatched Indrajit.
And when Indrajit fought, the monkeys were terrified and fled.
Then Hanumān, realizing that everyone had departed, perceived Rāvaṇa; having summoned and reprimanded the monkeys, he organized a great army, stood against the Ten-faced One, and cheered [them] on.
Then Indrajit fought while standing in the sky, and the monkeys did not see him.
Then Hanumān and Jāmbavat sprang into the sky and struck Indrajit with mountain peaks.
Then he fell to the earth, and Lakṣmaṇa dispatched him to the world of Yama.

Then Atikāya and Mahākāya, having slain the monkey army many times, afflicting Lakṣmaṇa, fighting with Rāma, and having captured Sugrīva, fought with Hanūmat and Jāmbavat; being defeated, those two warriors were seized, brought into the presence of Rāma, and presented to Rāma.
Rāma spoke to Atikāya:
"Tell me about Rāvaṇa's battle, that of his ministers, and of the other dreadful [warriors]."

Atikāya said: "Previously this was determined by us to be done, having divided the army: a mighty rākṣasa named Vidyunmālin, an extraordinary warrior who fights while visible and invisible, will fight alone against all the monkeys.
And other mighty and great [warriors], trained in weapons, have come; we two shall fight with you two. Rāvaṇa, ascending the Puṣpaka, will slay you from behind.
And other rākṣasas, led by Kumbhakarṇa, assuming your forms, will surround you, seize you, show you to Sītā, and kill you right before her."
Rāma said: "Ah, what is impossible for the powerful? The course of fate is crooked." Sugrīva, exceedingly furious, looked angrily and said to Rāma:
"These two deserve to be killed; they must not be released!"
Rāma said: "They are not to be killed; these two should be released. Bring garments and ornaments." As soon as this was said, they were brought by Hanumān, and Rāma gave them to the two.
[The two said:] "Bowing to you—that five-faced wooden log seen at the gate of Laṅkā: it was said by Śukra that when this is severed, Rāvaṇa will be killed.
And an ordinance uttered by the Bhārgava is written: 'Immediately after the cutting of the wood, one must go to the netherworld.'
Therefore, cleave this wood into five parts with a single effort, by the discharge of a single arrow; then, knowing your power, we shall fight very vigorously."

Then Rāma, understanding the words of the Bhārgava, strung the bow merely by touching the upper tip, fitted an arrow to the bow, and making it heard by the two rākṣasas and Hanumān, released the arrow.

The arrow sped from the bow. Those two rākṣasas, observing the path of the arrow and seeing the wood split into five by the arrow, petitioned Rāma: "Our children must be protected by you." Rāma said, "So be it." The two rākṣasas entered Laṅkā.

Then the monkeys went to fight on the rampart, leveled the entire enclosure with their heels, feet, knees, hands, and backs, and advanced to the second rampart. Then Rāvaṇa came, routed them all with arrows, and pursuing them, went toward Rāma.
Then he pierced Rāma as well with five arrows.
Then Rāma wounded Rāvaṇa with ten arrows.
A most dreadful battle took place between the two.
Rāvaṇa pierced [him] with ten arrows.
Then, his body wounded by Rāma's arrows, the rākṣasa became intent on fleeing.
The monkeys and Lakṣmaṇa slaughtered millions upon millions of rākṣasas.
Then on the following day, Vibhīṣaṇa reflected and said this to Rāvaṇa:

5.116.s:
tṛtīyopāyakālo'ya caturthaṃ na vicāraya
caturtho viparīto na śastaḥśastārthakāriṇaḥ
5.116.d:
तृतीयोपायकालोऽय चतुर्थं न विचारय
चतुर्थो विपरीतो न शस्तःशस्तार्थकारिणः
5.116.m: "This is the time for the third expedient; do not deliberate on the fourth. / The fourth is adverse, not recommended for one who seeks what is beneficial according to the treatises.

5.116.s:
parasya cā'tmanaḥ śaktiṃ viditvā cā'tmano'dhikām
tadā yuddhaṃ praśastaṃ syādviparītaṃ vināśakam
5.116.d:
परस्य चाऽत्मनः शक्तिं विदित्वा चाऽत्मनोऽधिकाम्
तदा युद्धं प्रशस्तं स्याद्विपरीतं विनाशकम्
5.116.m: Knowing the enemy's strength and one's own, and that one's own is greater, / only then is battle commended; the reverse brings destruction.

5.116.s:
rāmeṇa balinānaiva yuddhaṃ te durbalasya ca
ekeṣuvālihantā'sau vālirjñātastvayā purā
5.116.d:
रामेण बलिनानैव युद्धं ते दुर्बलस्य च
एकेषुवालिहन्ताऽसौ वालिर्ज्ञातस्त्वया पुरा
5.116.m: You, being weak, should not fight at all with the mighty Rāma. / He is the slayer of Vālin with a single arrow; Vālin was known to you previously.

5.116.s:
mārīcamekabāṇena bhavānapi palāyitaḥ
nihatā rākṣasāḥ śūrā indrajicca suto hataḥ
5.116.d:
मारीचमेकबाणेन भवानपि पलायितः
निहता राक्षसाः शूरा इन्द्रजिच्च सुतो हतः
5.116.m: With a single arrow [he slew] Mārīca; you too fled. / Brave rākṣasas have been slain, and your son Indrajit has been killed.

5.116.s:
vareṇyatritayaṃ bhagnaṃ tena yuddhaṃ ca naiva te
dāsabhāvamatho vā'pi dattvā sītāmathā'pnuhi
5.116.d:
वरेण्यत्रितयं भग्नं तेन युद्धं च नैव ते
दासभावमथो वाऽपि दत्त्वा सीतामथाऽप्नुहि
5.116.m: Your triad of boons is broken, so you should not fight with him at all. / Or else, adopting servitude and giving back Sītā, attain [peace].

5.116.s:
gopurasthaṃ tathā dāru pañcavaktramatheṣuṇā
ciccheda pañcadhā tena rāmastvāṃ mārayiṣyati
5.116.d:
गोपुरस्थं तथा दारु पञ्चवक्त्रमथेषुणा
चिच्छेद पञ्चधा तेन रामस्त्वां मारयिष्यति
5.116.m: Likewise, the five-faced wooden post standing at the gateway / he severed into five with an arrow; therefore Rāma will kill you.

5.116.s:
tvadarthaṃ bahavo naṣṭā nāśameṣyaṃti cāpare
eko nyāyaḥ sukhārthāya na ca mauḍhyaṃ sahodara
5.116.d:
त्वदर्थं बहवो नष्टा नाशमेष्यंति चापरे
एको न्यायः सुखार्थाय न च मौढ्यं सहोदर
5.116.m: Many have perished for your sake, and others will perish. / Justice alone brings happiness; folly does not, brother!

5.116.s:
mānuṣīṃ mṛtyusaṃyuktāmanicchantīṃ pativratām
patnīṃ balavataścāpi pūjayitvā visarjaya
5.116.d:
मानुषीं मृत्युसंयुक्तामनिच्छन्तीं पतिव्रताम्
पत्नीं बलवतश्चापि पूजयित्वा विसर्जय
5.116.m: Having honored her, release this mortal woman who brings death, who desires you not, who is devoted to her husband, / and who is the wife of a mighty man.

5.116.s:
anicchantyāḥ samāyoge bhavedduḥkhaparaṃparā
durgandhamalasaṃyukto nārīsaṅgo jugupsitaḥ
5.116.d:
अनिच्छन्त्याः समायोगे भवेद्दुःखपरंपरा
दुर्गन्धमलसंयुक्तो नारीसङ्गो जुगुप्सितः
5.116.m: Union with a woman who does not desire it results in a series of sorrows; / association with a woman is loathsome, filled with foul odor and filth.

5.116.s:
viraktiratha cejjātā duḥkhāyākāryavartanam
anurāgoyadi bhavenmaraṇaṃ narakaṃ tataḥ
5.116.d:
विरक्तिरथ चेज्जाता दुःखायाकार्यवर्तनम्
अनुरागोयदि भवेन्मरणं नरकं ततः
5.116.m: If detachment arises, persistence in improper conduct leads to grief; / if attachment should arise, death and hell follow from that.

5.116.s:
ātmano maraṇaṃ vyarthaṃ tasyāścādya samāgame
tyāgo vā maraṇaṃ tāta dharmapatnyāstathā bhavet
5.116.d:
आत्मनो मरणं व्यर्थं तस्याश्चाद्य समागमे
त्यागो वा मरणं तात धर्मपत्न्यास्तथा भवेत्
5.116.m: Your own death would be in vain today upon union with her; / or abandonment or death of your lawful wife would occur, dear brother.

5.116.s:
evamādi tathā'nyacca kaśmalaṃ saṃbhaviṣyati
anyadākhyāmi te vākyaṃ sarveṣāṃ ca priyaṃ hitam
5.116.d:
एवमादि तथाऽन्यच्च कश्मलं संभविष्यति
अन्यदाख्यामि ते वाक्यं सर्वेषां च प्रियं हितम्
5.116.m: Such and other degradation will come to pass. / I tell you another word, agreeable and beneficial to all:

5.116.s:
gatvā rāmāntikaṃ natvā stutvā vijñāpya rāghavam
kṣama rāma mahāvīra śaraṇāgatavatsala
5.116.d:
गत्वा रामान्तिकं नत्वा स्तुत्वा विज्ञाप्य राघवम्
क्षम राम महावीर शरणागतवत्सल
5.116.m: Having gone near Rāma, bowed down, praised, and petitioned the Rāghava: / 'Forgive us, Rāma, mighty hero, affectionate to those who seek refuge!

5.116.s:
tāmasā rākṣasāḥ sarve vayamete supāpinaḥ
sītāpahārajaṃ doṣaṃ tyaktvā putrānavehi naḥ
5.116.d:
तामसा राक्षसाः सर्वे वयमेते सुपापिनः
सीतापहारजं दोषं त्यक्त्वा पुत्रानवेहि नः
5.116.m: All of us rākṣasas are tāmasic, very sinful. / Setting aside the fault born of Sītā's abduction, look upon us as your sons!

5.116.s:
tvadadhīnā vayaṃ rāma rakṣa vā mārayecchayā
ityudīrya purastasya rāghavasya sthitā vayam
5.116.d:
त्वदधीना वयं राम रक्ष वा मारयेच्छया
इत्युदीर्य पुरस्तस्य राघवस्य स्थिता वयम्
5.116.m: We are under your control, Rāma; protect us or slay us according to your wish!' / Speaking thus, we who stand before that Rāghava

5.116.s:
sthirāyuṣo bhaviṣyāmaḥ sthirarājyā daśānana
athā'ha rāvaṇo vākyamaho no rākṣaso bhavān
5.116.d:
स्थिरायुषो भविष्यामः स्थिरराज्या दशानन
अथाऽह रावणो वाक्यमहो नो राक्षसो भवान्
5.116.m: shall have enduring life and an enduring kingdom, Ten-faced One!" / Then Rāvaṇa spoke these words: "Ah, you are no rākṣasa!

5.116.s:
na śūro rājadharmaṃ ca na ca jānāsi śāśvatam
paranārīparadravyapararājyaniṣevayā
5.116.d:
न शूरो राजधर्मं च न च जानासि शाश्वतम्
परनारीपरद्रव्यपरराज्यनिषेवया
5.116.m: You are not heroic, nor do you know the eternal duty of kings: / by enjoying another's wife, another's wealth, and another's kingdom,

5.116.s:
śūrāṇāmuttamo dharmo na ṣaṇḍhānāṃ bhavādṛśām
śatrupakṣaṃ samāligya nirgacchecchā hi cennṛpa
5.116.d:
शूराणामुत्तमो धर्मो न षण्ढानां भवादृशाम्
शत्रुपक्षं समालिग्य निर्गच्छेच्छा हि चेन्नृप
5.116.m:
"The highest duty of warriors is not for eunuchs like you.
If you wish to depart, king, embrace the enemy's side."

5.116.s: atha bibhīṣaṇo mandiraṃ gatvā rāmāntikaṃ gatvā taṃ śaraṇamabhajat
5.116.d: अथ बिभीषणो मन्दिरं गत्वा रामान्तिकं गत्वा तं शरणमभजत्
5.116.m: Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having gone to his palace and [then] having approached Rāma, took refuge in him.

5.116.s: atha rāvaṇaḥ purānnirgatya rāmeṇa lakṣmaṇavānarai rākṣasā api yuyudhire
5.116.d: अथ रावणः पुरान्निर्गत्य रामेण लक्ष्मणवानरै राक्षसा अपि युयुधिरे
5.116.m: Then Rāvaṇa went out of the city, and the rākṣasas too fought with Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the monkeys.

5.116.s:
atha rāvaṇaṃ mahābalaṃ hantumaśaktorāmo vibhīṣaṇamukhamavalokya taduktacihnapadaṃ
bāṇena nirbhidyāmārayat
5.116.d:
अथ रावणं महाबलं हन्तुमशक्तोरामो विभीषणमुखमवलोक्य तदुक्तचिह्नपदं
बाणेन निर्भिद्यामारयत्
5.116.m: Then Rāma, unable to slay the mighty Rāvaṇa, looked at Vibhīṣaṇa's face and, piercing the vulnerable spot indicated by him with an arrow, killed [him].

5.116.s:
atha kumbhakarṇo mahāgadāmādāya sarvaṃ niṣpādya vānarānanekaśo bhakṣayitvā
rāmottamāṅgaṃ gadayā'han
5.116.d:
अथ कुम्भकर्णो महागदामादाय सर्वं निष्पाद्य वानराननेकशो भक्षयित्वा
रामोत्तमाङ्गं गदयाऽहन्
5.116.m: Then Kumbhakarṇa, taking a great club, laying waste to all, and devouring monkeys by the scores, struck Rāma's head with his club.

5.116.s:
atha rāmo niśitabāṇaśatena tamahanmamāra kumbhakarṇaḥ
atha vibhīṣaṇena rāvaṇādeḥ śrāddhādikaṃ kārayitvā śivālayaṃ tannāmnā
sītāmagnipraveśaśuddhāmumāmaheśvarābhyāṃ namayitvā purahareṇa
5.116.d:
अथ रामो निशितबाणशतेन तमहन्ममार कुम्भकर्णः
अथ विभीषणेन रावणादेः श्राद्धादिकं कारयित्वा शिवालयं तन्नाम्ना
सीतामग्निप्रवेशशुद्धामुमामहेश्वराभ्यां नमयित्वा पुरहरेण
5.116.m:
Then Rāma struck him down with a hundred sharp arrows; Kumbhakarṇa died.

Then, having Vibhīṣaṇa perform the funeral rites and the rest for Rāvaṇa and others, and having a temple to Śiva built in his name,

having caused Sītā, purified by entering fire, to bow to Umā and Maheśvara, and having received from [Śiva], the destroyer of the cities,

5.116.s:
dattākhilāmṛtabalāyuṣyaḥ supuṣpakamāruhya jaladhimuttaryī pārāvārataṭe senāṃ
samavasthāpya śivapratiṣṭhāṃ tatra kṛtvā munibhirdevairabhyarcito'yodhyāmagamat
5.116.d:
दत्ताखिलामृतबलायुष्यः सुपुष्पकमारुह्य जलधिमुत्तर्यी पारावारतटे सेनां
समवस्थाप्य शिवप्रतिष्ठां तत्र कृत्वा मुनिभिर्देवैरभ्यर्चितोऽयोध्यामगमत्
5.116.m: all nectar, strength, and longevity, he mounted the splendid Puṣpaka, crossed the ocean, stationed the army on the seashore, established [a shrine to] Śiva there, and, worshipped by sages and gods, went to Ayodhyā.
Then, accompanied by Bharata and others, and worshipped by the citizens, Vasiṣṭha, and the sages, he went to his own palace.

Having himself worshipped the gods headed by Indra who had arrived, with seats and other honors, and having honored the monkeys, his matted locks loosened and [himself] consecrated in the kingdom, the gods, delighted by the slaying of Rāvaṇa, said to Rāma:

5.116.s:
tvayā'tmarājye sthāpitā vayaṃ naḥsarvadā paripālaya tvamādinārāyaṇo
devonikhiladuṣṭanigrahārthamavatīrṇo rāvaṇaṃ sabāndhavaṃ hatvā
lokatrayarakṣako'si śriyā saha sukhī bhavetyudīrya svargaṃ gatāḥ
5.116.d:
त्वयाऽत्मराज्ये स्थापिता वयं नःसर्वदा परिपालय त्वमादिनारायणो
देवोनिखिलदुष्टनिग्रहार्थमवतीर्णो रावणं सबान्धवं हत्वा
लोकत्रयरक्षकोऽसि श्रिया सह सुखी भवेत्युदीर्य स्वर्गं गताः
5.116.m: "We have been established in our own realm by you; protect us always. You are the primordial Nārāyaṇa, the Lord descended to subjugate all the wicked; having slain Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen, you are the protector of the three worlds. Be happy with Śrī!" Having spoken thus, they went to heaven.
Then the inhabitants of Ayodhyā, overjoyed, said to Rāma:

5.116.s:
hatvā śatrūnsamāyāto dṛṣṭvā prāpto'si vai śivam
diṣṭyā tvaṃ rājase rāma diṣṭyā pālayase prajāḥ
5.116.d:
हत्वा शत्रून्समायातो दृष्ट्वा प्राप्तोऽसि वै शिवम्
दिष्ट्या त्वं राजसे राम दिष्ट्या पालयसे प्रजाः
5.116.m: "Having slain your enemies, you have arrived; having seen [her], you have indeed attained auspiciousness! / By good fortune you shine, Rāma; by good fortune you protect your subjects.

5.116.s:
tvayāyajñāḥ kariṣyaṃte tvayā dharmovivardhate
itipauravacaḥśrutvārāmo rājīvalocanaḥ
5.116.d:
त्वयायज्ञाः करिष्यंते त्वया धर्मोविवर्धते
इतिपौरवचःश्रुत्वारामो राजीवलोचनः
5.116.m: Sacrifices will be performed by you; through you dharma flourishes." / Hearing these words of the citizens, lotus-eyed Rāma
honored all the citizens with garments and other gifts. / Having honored the sages along with all the people, the righteous-souled one said:
"Is your asceticism thriving? Has your sacrifice been performed well? / Are you devoted to your own wives? Is the Lord worshipped?
Do your wives have good offspring? Is everything exceedingly happy?"
The sages said: / "While you are king, O descendant of Kakutstha, all is well with the ascetics. / We are departing from this place; or what do you think, O king?"
Rāma said: / "He with whom the Brahmins are pleased, with him Śambhu is pleased. / He with whom the Lord is pleased, good fortune will be his.
Therefore, having taken a meal here, you should depart thereafter." / Saying "So be it," the multitudes of sages, having eaten an excellent meal
and honored him with blessings, joyfully went to their respective abodes. / Rāma too, exceedingly pleased, with his wife and along with his younger brother,
conducted a thornless reign, dear to all people. / Whatever sinner listens to this narrative,
freed from all sins, attains the supreme Brahman. / No misfortune will befall the man who remembers this,
and whoever proclaims it. Thus this has been declared.

5.117.m: Sūta said: / Having dined in the house of Bharadvāja, Rāmacandra of serene mind, / accompanied by the lord of sages, Viṣṇu, and joined by monkeys and bears,
when the sky was covered with clouds and the wind was blowing gently, / [saw] somewhere inside that forest the excellent house of Sudeva.

It was furnished with pillars of gold, framed with plates of gold,
adorned with jewels and pearls, and provided with silver pitchers,

fragrant with sandal, camphor, musk, and saffron,
fitted with lattices made of unguents, covered over with pieces [of cloth],

receiving the moon's radiance, with a central wall visible to the sun,
with the whole interior floor sprinkled with essence of moon-plant flowers,

and the entire northern direction entirely devoid of any wall,
with painted representations arranged on pillar after pillar at its very base.

Its courtyard measured a hundred cubits, fashioned upon crystal;
a pārijāta tree stood there, its shade extending beyond the courtyard of the mansion.

There was a dense banana grove there, entirely thriving in the rains,
accompanied by the banana grove and surrounded by a grove of ketakī plants,

filled with the cries of peacocks and the sweet humming of bees,
resonant with the sound of flocks of pigeons, and adorned with various orchards,

crowded with hundreds of mansions, resonant with intoxicated cuckoos,
with numerous trees adorned with great jewels dangling from their branches,

with the directions filled with the sounds of the songs of Kinnara women,
charming with its many pleasure groves, an excellent bank of the Gautamī,

the sacred house of Bhāradvāja, endowed with endless virtues,
attended by hundreds of male and female slaves resembling Rati and Madana,

provided with various implements, the auspicious house of Bhāradvāja.
Within it was a mansion, and inside it were domestic courtyards.

Among those eight, there was one house in the middle, exceedingly beautiful,
adorned on the four sides with temples and palaces dedicated to Mahādeva,

in each divine abode adorned with maidens and musical performances of singing, dancing, and instruments,
designed specifically for the rest of excellent celestial women.

Departing from Bhāradvāja's house accompanied by Śeṣa,
Rāma went to that great house of his situated in the middle of the forest.

Then, entering inside, which was spread with carpets and provided with distinct cloth seats,
and having one throne placed in the center, and many seats for the sages,

having first seated the narrator of the Purāṇas on an incomparable seat,
and then having seated the king, the chief monkeys, and bears on excellent seats, and then Vasiṣṭha and the foremost sages,

he seated Nārāyaṇa, the rulers of the earth, and the monkeys,
while he himself took a lowly seat. The sky was covered with clouds, the directions were clear, the earth bore beautiful flowers and sown seeds,

and the courtyard was neither hot nor cold, fragrant with the saṃtāna and dama flowers.
Then, looking upon Śambhu, Rāma spoke these words: 'Recite the story of Śaṅkara!

O best of sages, no satiety comes to me listening to the tale of Maheśa, which destroys heaps of sins.
Indeed, what did Maheśvara do, surrounded by the hosts of gods, in the hermitage of Gautama?'

Śiva said:
Relying upon the great lute, that son of Vāyu, standing firm, questioned Śiva:
'What fruit would there be in the worship of the Lord with wealth earned righteously, and tell me what fruit from that produced unjustly?

Or what fruit is there in offering what has been stolen, when offering goods that have been appropriated?
Tell me, O Lord, one by one, the answer to these questions; explain it quickly, O Śambhu.'

Then the Lord spoke to the monkey: 'I shall tell you everything, listen with concentrated mind.
By worshipping Sadāśiva, the unborn, with righteously acquired goods, Gautama indeed attained this sovereignty.

Formerly, there was a brāhmaṇa, the son of Maṅkaṇa, named Ākatha, a twice-born;
he obtained a virtuous wife named Suśobhanā. He was poor, full of compassion, eating on the sixth day, and bereft of his parents.

Having fasted for five days, he was just about to eat when an ascetic arrived.
The ascetic spoke sweetly to Ākatha: 'Having fasted for a month, I have come to you to eat.

I will stay and eat if you have food, O sage; I have no desire to eat from another house.'
Ākatha said: 'I have not eaten for five days, O best of the twice-born, and today on the sixth day food has come to me.

Then something beyond hesitation must be done by me. Come, I will wash your feet today.'
Saying 'Om,' with his pair of feet washed, that yogin desired to take food.

He ate that food on a banana leaf—cooked and prepared with ghee,
and well accompanied by wild forest vegetables, respectfully—leaving no remainder whatsoever of this food.

Then, seeing the sage well satisfied, the ascetic Ākatha was delighted along with his wife.
And having eaten, the ascetic went away, and Ākatha, his mind contented, performed japa.

He adopted the gleaning livelihood of a pigeon with his wife for the expansion of his penance, that virtuous sage.
Then, placing Śiva, the lord of Umā, on a pedestal, he worshipped him in the liṅga, accompanied by his attendants.

Having installed the liṅga, as he was looking, he saw an unknown, emaciated brāhmaṇa,
naked, devoid of feet, one-eyed, with a deformed hand, earless, a master,
chanting Sāmans, well-versed in many scriptures, coming to the house.
Then Ākatha said this to his wife Suśobhanā:
'Indeed, a brāhmaṇa of deformed appearance is coming.

"Half the meal should be given to him, and protect the [other] half of the food; and on this sixth day, due to lack of food, life does not remain in you—this is how it appears to me; but what do you think? Speak."

Śobhanā said: 'The lifespan written on the forehead does not perish midway.'

'Just as, even though the sacrifice had a fixed span of life, its head was cut off by Vīrabhadra, although it had an eternal soul,
Or if food is to be given to him by me, my duty is according to your desire.'
The wife said: 'How could I eat while you have not eaten? Have I ever eaten first? Listen to this further:

Food is the life-breath of living beings, manifest to all embodied creatures.
Therefore, whoever gives food is called a giver of life-breath.

From food beings are born, and through it they indeed grow;
therefore, there is no gift higher than food, possessing great fruit.

When life is like a drop of water clinging to the tip of a trembling leaf of the sacred fig tree,
if one does not give, his birth is utterly useless.

Dharma is indeed the companion to the other world, not a wife, nor kinsmen;
wife, parents, or sons are not companions beyond the span of life.

Wealth, youth, and friends exist for welfare here, but dharma is situated for the benefit of both here and beyond.
O best of upholders of dharma, when another eats our [food], what is it to both of us?'
Hearing his wife's words, Ākatha, an ocean of compassion, / without any hesitation gave him the plentiful food. / This was Lord Śaṅkara who had come in various forms.
Having resolved thus in his mind, [he approached] his sin-destroying body.

Washing his feet up to the knees, and then washing the calves further above,
and washing the ankles below them, he offered the twice-born water to sip.

Then Ākatha brought an artificial foot into the courtyard of the house;
releasing the artificial foot, he sat down upon the offered seat.

Worshipping him properly, Ākatha fed that sage.
In the meantime, a madman arrived at the house.

Taking the artificial foot, he carried it outside the house;
then he set fire to that house and struck the husband and wife.

The brāhmaṇa Ākatha, being struck, entered the burning house at that time
swiftly to rescue the lord, the god Īśāna.
Then, having taken the Great Lord whose worship-offering was burnt, that best of the twice-born / went out and saw the anguish of his [wife's] face.
Rejecting the burnt worship-offering and seeing his burnt body as well, / the righteous one said to his wife: "Just as the worship of the Great Lord,
so all my limbs must without hesitation be made [burnt]." / Vyaṅgā said: "Even performed later, worship will be fruitful for you.
Just as upon the burning of other property, similar [property] is given by people, / so upon the burning of a worship-offering, the worship of that [Lord] should be performed [again]."

Ākatha said: "By means of articles acquired even by theft, worship does not bring welfare, / nor does worship of Śambhu performed with unjustly acquired [articles] bestow auspiciousness, O Brahmin lady."
Having said this, Ākatha quickly began to burn his own body; / taking the burned liṅga, that madman vanished in an instant.
Then Vyaṅgā, becoming Hara, restrained Ākatha: / "Why do you grieve, O Brahmin? I am a giver of boons; choose a boon!"
Ākatha too chose unwavering devotion to the feet of the Lord. / Sūta said: Having heard this story, Rāma, delighted, surrounded by sages,
bowed to Bharadvāja and asked permission for departure.
Then the sage Bharadvāja, pleased, bowed to Śambhu, to Vasiṣṭha the foremost of sages, / to Nārāyaṇa, and to the hosts of ṛṣis, and dismissed them; having bowed, they too departed.
The residents of Naimiṣa said: / Having gone to Ayodhyā, accompanied by all the sages, / what did the glorious Rāma and that renowned Śambhu do next?
Sūta said: / On the following day, Rāghava, desiring to perform the monthly śrāddha of Kausalyā, / invited the foremost twice-born who were like ṛṣis:
Śambhu the knower of all reality, Nārada, Romaśa, Bhṛgu, / and Viśvāmitra. Then Rāma, observing the vow of a single meal,
slept on a comfortably spread spot on the ground, with his senses calm. / Then, when the next day arrived, having bathed at dawn, knowing the rites,
he had pure food, vegetables, and the like prepared by the people: / various and wondrous kinds of cooked grains, suckable foods, and likewise
cakes and similar edibles—he had thirty-eight varieties prepared, / six kinds of milk-rice, two hundred [dishes of] cooked vegetables,
and three hundred varieties of uncooked mixed salads he prepared, / vegetables such as kālaśāka, and diverse fruits,
roots, single tubers, and bark-roots. Having had these prepared, Rāghava, / going to the river together with his brothers and family priest,
bathed in the waters of the Sarayū, made offerings into the fire, and welcomed the arriving twice-born; / having said "Welcome!" to them, the king, having performed the worship of the gods,
restraining his breath and making the formal resolve, gave the ritual invitation. / Rāma invited Romaśa and Nārada for the Vaiśvadeva rite;
he invited Śambhu, Bhṛgu, and the descendant of Kuśika in the place of the mothers. / Then, having made a ritual circle with cowdung and worshipped them suitably,
he washed their feet with water poured by Sītā. / Having made those Brahmins sip water, as he was about to enter the house,
a guest arrived: an old man of deformed appearance, / emaciated, his limbs trembling violently, his feet and head shaking,
afflicted by panting, coughing, and the like from the pulling of his sagging skin, / his cheeks moistened with rheum, and his beard smeared with saliva.
He said to King Rāma: "I am a lone brāhmaṇa who has arrived. / Food should also be given to me, an old and emaciated man."
Hearing his words, Rāma too spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa: / "Wash his feet; I shall worship the brāhmaṇa."
The guest then spoke agitatedly to Rāma: / "My eating is desired [only] when my feet are washed by you.
Are the [other] brāhmaṇas superior to me, that you slight me? / Do you not know the rules of the ancestral rite observed by the host of great sages?
From disrespecting me comes disrespect to all brāhmaṇas; / and your ancestral rite will be ruined, and you will go to hell."
Then Rāma himself washed the brāhmaṇa's feet; / having made that brāhmaṇa sip water, he then led him into the house.
Rāma himself, having sipped water, then gave him a seat of grass; / and when the brāhmaṇas were seated, restraining his breath,
and having obtained permission to perform his rite, he should then scatter water with sesamum / at the doorway with the mantra beginning 'apahata'.

Likewise, he should cast [water] at the place of the ancestors' vessel with [the mantra] 'udīratām'; / and with the Gāyatrī he should cast water with unbroken grain at the place of the gods' vessel; / and having sprinkled the cooked food, he should utter this mantra:

Having meditated on Gayā as the ground of the ancestral rite, having meditated on the god Janārdana, / and having meditated on the ancestors as the Vasus and others, he should then commence the ancestral rite.
He should perform the worship of the Viśvedevas with barley or with grains of rice; / then, taking two kuśa blades joined from base to tip together with unbroken grain,
with his right knee touching the ground, he makes the offering of water into the brāhmaṇa's hand: / 'This is indeed the seat of the Purūravas-Ārdrava gods.'
Having thus given their seat, the performer of the ancestral rite should request their momentary attention.
Then, after preparing the respectful offering on kuśa blades with tips pointing north, / and having turned the vessel downward, and [placing] a kuśa knot on top,
having then turned it upward and sprinkled it with golden water, / in the vessel lined with the purifying strainer he should pour water with the mantra beginning 'śaṃ no devī'.
The entire rite concerning the Viśvedevas [is performed] as enjoined by rule; / with the mantra 'You are barley, the king of grains', he should cast barley into the vessel.

He should then give small water jars mixed with honey along with fragrant paste and flowers; / having said, 'O brāhmaṇa, let this be the respectful offering for you,' and from him [receiving the reply,] 'Let there be the respectful offering,'
having asked, 'Shall I invoke the gods?', and after receiving the reply to that, / having recited 'viśve devāsaḥ', he should scatter kuśa grass upon the head of the brāhmaṇa.
He should silently recite: 'O Viśvedevas, hear this [prayer] of mine; let them come.' / Having arrived and sat down, he should then bring the vessel with darbha grass.
Then, having poured water from the principal vessel onto the right foot, / [he places it] on the purifying strainer pointing eastward in the brāhmaṇa's right hand;

with the mantra beginning 'yā divyāḥ', he should pour that vessel-water; / having said, 'Sir, this is the respectful offering,' and from him [receiving the reply,] 'Indeed, let there be the respectful offering,'
and holding the respectful water in the vessel, he should set that vessel somewhere; / then, having given water in his hand, he should worship these [gods] with barley.
Having asked, 'Do you worship? Worship!', and after the reply from him, / having worshipped from the feet to the crown of the head, the giver of water then,
with the mantra beginning 'gandhadvārām', upon his replying 'So be it', / should likewise perform the worship of the ancestors, worn over the right shoulder.
Having made the brāhmaṇa wear his sacred thread over the left shoulder, [taking] broken kuśa blades mixed with sesamum, / and placing his left knee upon the ground, he should give that seat.
Facing south, he should then ask for their momentary attention; / on darbha blades with tips pointing south, he should place the three vessels face down.
He should then set them face up, joined with a knot of three kuśa blades; / then, having sprinkled [water] in the vessels containing the purifying strainer and sesamum,

having poured water with the mantra beginning 'śaṃ no devī', he should scatter sesamum seeds with 'You are sesamum'; / then, having given fragrant paste and flowers, he asks: 'Is the offering agreeable?'
Having received the reply, 'Let there be the offering', he should then invoke the ancestors; / standing with sesamum, flowers, and kuśa, holding the prepared respectful offering in his hand,

with the mantra beginning 'uśantas tvā', he should offer the water of the respectful offering three times; / the worship of them, however, is [done with sacred thread] over the right shoulder, just as before.
Having washed it, he should provide a golden vessel for the gods; / for the ancestors he should provide a silver one, or according to what is available.
In the absence of that, bell-metal not eaten from by another is excellent; / in the absence of that, vessels of palāśa wood are not mediocre.
Leaves of plantain, mango, jambu, puṃnāga, / parāka, campaka, madhūka, and kuṭaja,
and the leaves of citron should indeed be given by men in an ancestral rite. / Then, taking food with a ladle, and ghee with both hands,
with his sacred thread worn over the right shoulder, he should then ask the brāhmaṇa about serving: / 'I shall perform the offering into the fire'; and the reply to that is: 'Perform it.'

Having served, he should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder; having sprinkled ghee over it, he should take it up; / he should sacrifice, uttering: 'To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Reverence!'
With 'To Yama, descendant of Aṅgiras, accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Reverence!', / having offered the second oblation and sprinkled unbroken grain with ghee, then,

thereafter with 'To Agni the bearer of funeral offerings, svadhā! Reverence!'; / having sacrificed, and having placed the thread over the right shoulder, and served food, he should approach the brāhmaṇas.
With the wooden stirring-stick he should then repeatedly drop [food] into the ancestors' vessel; / the remainder is for the vessel of funeral cakes, and then the washing of the ladle,
then the throwing of the stirring-stick into the fire; then he should spread a base for the vessels; / and on the right side of the vessel he should immediately give food.
He gave all the chewable foods, eatables, and vegetables; / then the very aged guest, looking this way and that,
said to the gentle Rāghava: "Quickly bow down! / Hunger is upon us; shall I eat by your command?"
Rāma spoke these words: "Wait a moment, O sage; / the deities and ancestors are now about to be quickly bowed to by me."

Having said this, Rāghava then gave the food that was in the bowl; / [spreading] kuśa grass with tips pointing east and north in the rites for gods, and with tips pointing west and south [in those for ancestors].
in the rite for the ancestors, the darbha blades as purifying strainers, barley and also sesamum; / they make the offering of food with the mantra beginning 'pṛthivī'.
Touched by the brāhmaṇa's thumb with the mantra 'idaṃ viṣṇuḥ', / he should first give to the gods, reciting 'ye devāḥ'.
Then he should give to the ancestors, and then he should give to the guest; / having uttered the words beginning with 'To the deities', he should give water for sipping before eating.

Having silently recited the Gāyatrī three times, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder and facing forward, / wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should thereafter recite the three verses beginning with 'madhu'.
Having said to them, 'Eat!', while the brāhmaṇas are eating, / causing chewables, eatables, and the like to be served, reciting the demon-slaying mantras—
meanwhile, that brāhmaṇa who was the guest performed / such a great wonder that I shall tell it in brief:
in a single mouthful he swallowed everything that was in the vessel, / and said: "Let enough be given for the life-breath oblations!
Unable to give even this much, why did you undertake the ancestral rite? / You are unable to provide for me alone, Rāma; why in vain
did you undertake to provide food for many, Rāma, in vain? / Actions undertaken rashly do not reach completion.
What was prepared by you is not enough for all my life-breath oblations! / How can a meal be given to me, and how to these? Speak!"
Heroic Rāma said to him: "Eat indeed as you please!" / Having said this, he looked upon that supreme wonder of an act of his.
Then, summoning Śambhu, he said: 'Serve [the food]. / You are the father, and goddess Śivā, Pārvatī, is the mother; such is my thought.
Goddess Annapūrṇeśvarī is Bhavānī herself; such is my thought.' / That consort of Śambhu spoke these words: 'I shall give enough of it.'
Then Umā, taking a bell-metal vessel filled with boiled rice and adorned, / and taking with a golden ladle fragrant, radiant milk-rice,
gave the milk-rice, saying: 'May this become inexhaustible for him!' / She placed it honorably and joyfully into the right hand of the twice-born.
Shaking his head, he then looked upward; / having received the milk-rice in his hand, his hand remained outstretched.
'Let the delicious milk-rice be served! But why is this cooked [only] so-so?' / Śambhu's wife said to him: 'Eat what is in your hand; then I will give more.'
Then the brāhmaṇa ate what was on the palm of his hand again. / Realizing it was inexhaustible, he then stretched out his other [hand].
The goddess gave milk-rice into that palm as well; / indeed, the chaste woman also gave inexhaustible cooked food to the other brāhmaṇas.
Then, knowing that the milk-rice in both hands had become inexhaustible, / and seeing another hand, the twice-born then extended it.
He said: 'Food must be given, excellent, along with pulse soup and clarified butter.' / Goddess Śivā, the beloved of Śambhu, gave it inexhaustibly in the same manner.
Whatever the virtuous woman gave at that time, all of it was inexhaustible. / Another hand was then produced, filled again and again.
Having thus manifested a thousand hands, he ceased, / and the brāhmaṇa spoke this word: 'Give me water for rinsing the mouth; / I am satisfied by you, auspicious lady, not by Rāma, nor by Sītā.'
Śambhu said: 'Where food was given by Rāma and by Sītā, it was given by me. / Beyond this, what else should be given, or is it complete? Tell me!'
The twice-born said: 'I am satisfied; nothing more is to be given to me. And what remains in my hand, / O learned one, since it is on the hand, it never fell off in any way.
Sitting, he reflected for a long time: 'How is it that I have only [one] hand? / All this was done for eating, not for any other action of mine.
Therefore, through another action, all of this will become empty.' / Having resolved this in his mind, the guest had his limbs smeared [with food].
While all the gods watched, it became like a wonder. / Then, knowing the twice-born were satisfied, Rāghava, knower of the highest truth,
holding the ladle, asked according to rule: 'Are you satisfied?' / Saying, 'We are satisfied,' the foremost twice-born scattered the food with mantras.
Facing south, he should offer the rice-ball near the vessel; / he should also arrange water for rinsing the mouth for the brāhmaṇas right there.
Into leaf-vessels of leftover food, they rinsed their mouths; / and those twice-born entered another room, but without the guest.
The guest said: 'Rinsing of the mouth must be done outside by me, O ruler of subjects! / I am unable to stand up; give me your hand, O Rāghava!'
Then Rāma offered his hand, but the excellent twice-born did not rise. / Then Hanūmān also powerfully gave him his hand.
Grasping the eminent twice-born with the other hand, / the king of monkeys pulled him up, but the twice-born cried out with a shout:
The twice-born said: 'Clearly my hand is being broken! Raise me from somewhere else!' / Wrapping him along with his seat up to his head with his tail by force,
Then he ran swiftly, but the twice-born did not move at all; / then the heroic monkey tore at the earth with his feet.
and, firmly planting both feet, cast down the head of the twice-born. / The house shattered, and all the twice-born [went] outside as well.
Then that Hanūmān went outside together with the old twice-born, / and he placed the emaciated, aged brāhmaṇa on a seat.
Taking water in an earthen jar for the twice-born, / Jāmbavān said: 'O brāhmaṇa, clear water along with a vessel must be taken by you.
Sītā should wash your limbs, and Lakṣmaṇa should be the water-giver.' / Jāmbavān told Rāma everything that was spoken by the brāhmaṇa.
To wash the twice-born, Rāma commanded his younger brother and his beloved. / Saumitri took the water, and likewise for washing the limbs of the twice-born,
he washed his entire body, like an image of the king of the earth. / Then, at Rāma's instruction, the two of them did just that.
Then the guest released the rinse from his own mouth onto Sītā's face. / Covered with water, the adorned, chaste lady washed it.
The face of the twice-born was filled with abundant mucus and saliva; that chaste lady / wiped it, and having washed it again, removed the nasal mucus.
Having made him rinse his mouth, Saumitri said to the twice-born: 'Stand up!' / The twice-born said, 'It is not possible!' Then Hanūmān also arrived.
The guest, the brāhmaṇa, said to him: 'I have been hurt by Hanūmān; / while seizing and lifting me previously, I was dropped by the monkey.'
Then Jāmbavān said to him: 'My hairy body is indeed soft; / now you shall be held by me, O brāhmaṇa, and there will be no pain.'
Having said this, Jāmbavat took hold of the brāhmaṇa with both arms and lifted him up; / then, holding the hem of the twice-born's garment, he set that sage down.
Then Rāma performed circumambulation around the foremost twice-born; / having received blessings from the foremost twice-born and having offered betel beforehand,
Rāma, taking hold of his feet together with his brothers, said: / 'O Sītā, the body of this guest was not washed by you!
There is impurity on both shanks of this guest, and his mouth is covered with impurity. / Wash his face thoroughly; the twice-born cannot bear impurity.'
Sītā said: 'It was thoroughly washed, and now it has come out again.' / Rāma said: 'Wash the impurity again, otherwise there would be fault on my part.'
Then, having done so, Sītā remained completely silent. / Extremely enraged, the twice-born spoke to Rāma and Sītā:
'Sītā should hold those feet of mine, O king of kings! / You should [hold] the hands, and Bharata should provide me fanning!
Lakṣmaṇa should be the arranger of my mass of hair, / and Śatrughna must clean my mucus with his own cloth!'
Sūta said: / Then they did everything spoken by the guest in that way; / and the twice-born, men, monkeys, and rākṣasas were filled with astonishment.
Goddess Śivā and Śambhu looked on with knitted brows, / and in their minds they both spoke: 'The guest is Śambhu himself!'
And the guest became gracious, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / dressed in yellow garments, adorned on all his limbs, and exceedingly radiant.
Śambhu, the three-eyed lord, who was propitiated formerly, became pleased; / resembling pure crystal, he was adorned with all ornaments,
resembling ten million suns, wearing a diadem, an ocean of compassion. / Supporting the hand of the wielder of the discus, Sadāśiva stood firm.
Rāma, of supreme righteous soul, with his body bristling with horripilation, / fell like a staff upon the earth, his eyes overflowing with bliss.
His brothers bowed down like staffs, lying on the surface of the earth. / Śiva raised the descendant of Kakutstha, embraced him, and smelled his head,
and spoke sweet words to Rāma, the lotus-eyed. / Śiva said: 'Choose a boon! I am pleased, [a boon] difficult to attain even for Brahmā and others.
There is nothing that I should withhold from you; choose without delay!' / Glorious Rāma said: 'O Lord of the Universe, earthly kingship is not to be asked for by me now;
and heaven is obtained through actions; devotion [arises] from the sight of your feet. / Look, I enjoy health, and that Sītā is the best of women.'
All kings have been brought under control, and the subjects are endowed with dharma. / Joy indeed has come to me from your arrival, O Acyuta.
Even so, grant me a boon: let my devotion to you remain steadfast, / and likewise, O Lord, remain in my house for three years, O Master,
expounding all dharmas in this very form, O Śaṅkara!” / Śiva said: “So be it, O Rāma; everything shall come to pass for you.”
Then the bearer of the discus spoke to king Rāma, the lotus-eyed: / “Choose a boon, O fortunate one! I am pleased; whatever you desire [is yours].”
Śrī Rāma spoke these words: “Indeed, there is nothing for me to ask, / for whatever was to be obtained has been obtained from Śambhu; everything else has been declared.
Yet I ask for one thing, O Viṣṇu: be always pleased [with me].” / Then Hari said to Sītā: “I am now pleased with you.
Choose a boon; I grant it.” Then Sītā said this: / “A boon was chosen earlier by my husband, and no other boon is desirable to me.
If you would grant a wish, let my mind ever turn away / from any other man. Homage be to you, O Lord of the twice-born!”
Then all those sages bowed down to the two foremost deities. / Then he said to Rāghava: “Dine together with your kinsmen.
I shall dwell in your delightful, secluded palace together with the goddess; / Viṣṇu, the cause of all, accompanied by the daughter of the ocean,
shall stay in one palace, O Rāma, for he is longing [to do so].” / Then, in a pure, spacious mansion furnished with seats and filled with many vessels,
the divine sage Vasiṣṭha sat before the two, / and the other ṛṣis, all in order of seniority, as did the kings.
Facing them, king Rāma, together with his brothers, / seated them on seats that were youthful and equal in portion.
Consoling his servants headed by Hanūmat, Rāma said: / "May you all wait; I shall eat afterwards, and not otherwise."
Then they all presented water for the feet and guest-offerings in due order, / and all those who were attendants of Rāma also dined.
Having given them betel, he then fed the lords of the monkeys and others. / When all had dined, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
having given food to the wretched, the blind, the destitute, and others, / and to beasts, birds, and deer, began to worship the twilight.
Having performed the twilight prayers, recitation, and other rites, and then bowed to them, the king, / Rāma, went to the throne, attended by the citizens, countryfolk, and others.
Going to the assembly hall, that Rāghava shone / like the god, the husband of Śacī, surrounded by all the gods.
Having performed all royal duties along with his brothers, / that Rāghava dismissed them all, one by one, by name.
He dismissed his brothers, the monkeys, and others as well. / Then Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great splendor, spoke these words to Rāma:
“Do not forget what duty you have at dawn, O Rāghava! / Śambhu, the Lord of the world, the divine husband of Ambikā, is staying [here].
The Lord must be remembered and revered with care.” / Saying, “So be it,” to the guru and bowing to him, the king dismissed him.
“Having risen at dawn, O guru, what did Rāma, the best of the wise, / do? Tell us that, for our curiosity to hear is indeed great.”

Sūta said: / “Then, having looked upon Śambhu, Rāma spoke: ‘Recount the story of Śaṅkara! / Satiety has not arisen in me, O best of sages, while hearing the glorification of Maheśa, which destroys heaps of sins.’
Śambhu said: / ‘Now I shall tell you the remainder of the question, the answer spoken by the Lord: / Those who worship the Lord with goods acquired unjustly are born deformed.
For instance: a certain rākṣasa named Rūpaka, having worshiped Śaṅkara with goods acquired unjustly, made a bell for the pleasure of the Lord with that very property.
His son was known as Sampāti; / he worshiped Śaṅkara with [goods] acquired through theft.
Both of them died on the same day, went to the realm of Śiva, and were addressed by Vīrabhadra:
“O Rūpaka, worship and the bell and other items were offered by you with goods acquired unjustly; because of that disposition, you will become a deformed attendant of thieves.
Because you did not clearly hear the name from the utterance of Śiva's abode, / his ear was destroyed by its sound; vision was not impaired to this extent, O god, by your proper worship of the Lord.
Therefore, devotion will exist [for you].” Vīrabhadra then commanded: “Become an attendant named Anaśana wandering somewhere!”
And the two, having become so, remained in the realm of Śiva.’
Śambhu said: / ‘Now I shall relate to Hanumat the story spoken by Maheśa concerning worship with defiled goods.
Listen, O Rāghava; I shall explain the conduct of the Pramathas and the ripening of karma for each one.’
Asked by Hanumat, “May an explanation be given of the attendants with afflicted limbs,” Śiva said:
‘Listen, O wise one, to this which is said concerning whoever knowingly offers defiled goods to the Lord:

This one is seen covered with sweat on all his limbs at all times, with his clothes wet with sweat, his body having a small stream produced by sweat, drops of sweat falling from the tip of his nose, unfit for touch.
Formerly he performed the worship of the Lord while sweating. / In this connection, I shall relate a legendary history:
There was a brāhmaṇa farmer known as Cekitāna. / Daily producing crops, bathing every morning regularly,
when midday arrived, this brāhmaṇa, performing his recitation, / spoke to his wife: “Bring food for me quickly!”
With the food brought by her, he performed the worship of Śiva in haste, / scorched by the sun and sweating all over,
with fragrances, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and the like, accompanied by drops of sweat. / Then, when the evening arrived, his body washed and well-adorned,
he worshiped the Lord of the gods with materials suited to the time. / Then, that one of great intellect died and went to the realm of Śiva.
And he was told by Vīrabhadra: “Become a sweating attendant! / Formerly Śambhu was worshiped [by you] with articles touched by sweat,

and you were always full of sweat; therefore, become a sweat-attendant!”’ / Śambhu said: ‘Commanded by the hero, this attendant came [here], O Rāma.

"Look at this Ghaṇṭāmukha! Formerly he was a righteous vaiśya named Vibhāvasu, a maker of great gifts, who daily fed brāhmaṇas, performed his observances, and having bowed to Śiva in the morning and worshipped him with flowers...
having smeared a certain place with cow dung, procured lotuses and other items, and offered them to the God, he sounded a defiled bell.’
Rāma said: / ‘How was the bell defiled?’
Śambhu said: / ‘Formerly there was a certain boy well known as Soma. / And he had a son named Manda, ten years of age.
And he, O king, threw boiled gruel cooked on fire into the bell, / and even ate them [from it]; thereby it became defiled.
Endeavoring to seize it, he then said this to the vaiśya. / Then the vaiśya himself, having determined the purification of the article there,
performed it in ordinary worldly affairs, entering the status of worldly transaction. / Through this connection with sin, he became an attendant with the face of a bell.’
Rāma said: / Since the purification of wealth is pure, how was it the cause of sin? / It is well said that through the purification of wealth—how does it not purify wealth?
Śambhu said: / In worldly conduct he will not become your devotee; / he goes to Śiva's abode, and the speaker likewise will be so.
Sūta said: / And whoever narrates this story, there is no one equal to him on earth; / it is the most secret of secrets, O brāhmaṇas, granting knowledge of Śiva.
This has been told to you, O brāhmaṇas, most meritorious, conferring long life, and great; / whoever listens to this with devotion is glorified in the world of Śiva.
To the reciter of the Purāṇa should be given cloth, cows, gold, and ornaments; / land endowed with grain and fruit should be given according to one's capacity.
The dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava destroys the flood of all sins; / whoever reads it or listens to it attains the supreme state.

6.0.m: The glorious Padma Purāṇa. / The Uttarakhaṇḍa.
